transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-17 15:30 UTC / Duration: ~48m / Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Nina Gomez (Redwood CSM), Rajiv Menon (Polaris, Head of ML), Sophie Park (Platform), Carlos Ortiz (SRE), Ava Li (CTO)

Summary: quick postmortem follow-up from last week where Polaris saw a steady memory growth on their Dedicated pool causing OOM kills and fallback to hosted that bumped latency. Today is to review mitigations, share traces, confirm rollback/fallback policy, and agree next steps.

Topics: memory regression timeline, KV cache behavior, batch sizing, fallback pool policy, alerting thresholds, security notes (KMS/audit logs), canary test plan, cost impact.

[00:00] Laura Chen: all right everyone thanks for making time. we wanted to follow up on last weeks incident where a memory leak surfaced on your dedicated pool, and make sure folks have the artifacts they need and that the fallback policy behaved as expected.
[00:18] Rajiv Menon: thanks Laura, and hi team. yeah, friday was a rough morning. we had a slow ramp of memory over ~4 hours and then pods started OOMing, the platform then fell back to hosted which kept us up but latency spiked and cost went up.
[00:32] Marcus Patel: quick note — from the Redwood serving side we observed the KV cache retention growth correlated with long-running sessions and a particular model variant. not saying that's causal yet but it's our first hypothesis.
[00:48] Carlos Ortiz: just to add, our histograms showed a growth of resident memory on the nodes, not just the container. so we suspected either driver-level pinned pages or a native lib leak.
[01:05] Sophie Park: apologies if im fuzzy, can you restate the model variant? we have a bunch of pinned model hashes in Dedicated.
[01:12] Marcus Patel: sure, the telemetry points to model: openlm-30b-v2-quant which you rolled yesterday. the sequence length distribution shifted too — more long sequences plus continuous conversations which amplified cache pressure.
[01:30] Ava Li: right — we did push that variant because of quality, but we didn't expect this kind of resource profile.
[01:38] Laura Chen: high level recap of what our runbooks did: when capacity hit the configured memory threshold, the Redwood fleet attempted graceful eviction and then routing policy diverted new requests to the fallback hosted cluster. that kept customer experience mostly up but you saw latency and some 5xx from the transformation layer.
[01:58] Rajiv Menon: the fallback logic worked but we need a tighter SLA on failover time and more transparent cost visibility. the billing spike surprised product folks.
[02:10] Nina Gomez: noted — we will include cost delta metrics in the postmortem doc. also, we can add a cost-alert channel to notify you proactively when fallback is triggered.

[02:28] Marcus Patel: i want to walk through the traces we collected. i uploaded two artifacts to the shared drive: heap-dump-11-14.bin and kernel-trace-11-14.txt, link in the notes. the heap dumps show incremental allocations in the custom CUDA allocator path plus increased KV cache entries. there are a few hotspots in an attention kernel that call into our c++ shim.
[02:52] Carlos Ortiz: a lot of the allocator churn lines up with our long-running sessions that don't call end_session, maybe the client lib not clearing prefixes correctly. we do see client-side keep-alives extending sessions.
[03:10] Rajiv Menon: is the session/keepalive thing something on our side or is it Redwood's session handling?
[03:16] Marcus Patel: it's a mix. the Redwood serving runtime keeps a KV cache for active conversations; if client session tokens never expire then cache entries persist longer. but there's also a leak in the native path exacerbating it. so both need addressing.
[03:30] Sophie Park: ok so short term we should tune session TTLs and enable more aggressive cache eviction — that likely curbs the growth while a deeper patch lands.
[03:40] Marcus Patel: yes. recommended immediate mitigations: reduce KV cache TTL from 6h to 30m for that namespace, enable periodic background compaction, and temporarily increase GC frequency on dedicated nodes.
[03:55] Laura Chen: operationally we can push a config change for you in Dedicated, or hand off the exact helm manifests for your infra team to apply. which do you prefer?
[04:05] Sophie Park: we'd like to do it ourselves, but can you produce a diffs/manifest example and a one-click rollback plan? we've had automation scares before.
[04:16] Nina Gomez: absolutely — we'll send a patch PR and a rollback script. Marcus will include the exact linted helm patch.

[04:30] Carlos Ortiz: also, i want to talk about alerting thresholds. our current threshold was a single node 85% mem used for 10 minutes. by the time that hit it was already in a non-linear phase. can we get earlier warning?
[04:44] Marcus Patel: yes — recommended is two-stage alerts: one at 60% with rate-of-change slope detection (e.g., 20% growth over 30m) and another at 75% sustained. we can export that rule for your Prometheus.
[05:00] Rajiv Menon: great, please include histograms so we can see per-session tail latencies.

[05:12] Ava Li: quick security question — during fallback the data path hit hosted infra, is our data encrypted on egress and how are keys rotated? the security team raised concerns.
[05:22] Laura Chen: good question. by default all egress is TLS and we support customer-managed keys for encryption at rest via KMS. the hosted fallback respects your data residency and PII redaction config; we'll include the specific audit log entries for the fallback window.
[05:40] Sophie Park: can you also confirm if HSM-backed keys are used in the hosted option?
[05:45] Marcus Patel: yes we can enable HSM KMS for your tenant; in the fallback flow we use the same encryption keys if you have Customer Managed Keys configured. if not, we'd use Redwood-managed keys — we'll document the exact log lines.

[06:00] Rajiv Menon: back to remediation timeline — whats the expected ETA on a code patch for the native leak?
[06:06] Marcus Patel: we have a two-track plan: immediate mitigations (config/TTL/eviction) which we can push in 24-48 hours; medium-term kernel fix to the C++ shim which we think is a 2-week work item including QA; long-term is runtime rewrite for that allocator path which is a quarter-level project.
[06:27] Carlos Ortiz: can we get a canary release after the kernel fix? we want to validate under your load generator then mirror it in our staging.
[06:34] Marcus Patel: absolutely — standard canary with 10% traffic to a patched node group, synthetic load to mimic your long conversations, and we will supervise.

[06:48] Laura Chen: i want to talk about the fallback policy itself. currently you had a fallback to hosted with default routing; we can make the fallback smarter — e.g., route only non-latency-sensitive routes or degrade batch sizes.
[07:02] Sophie Park: that's interesting, we have an internal route for tokenization and a separate high-priority latency-sensitive inference. can Redwood route by route?
[07:10] Marcus Patel: yes, per-route routing is supported. you can tag routes with priority levels and a policy will route low-priority traffic to the hosted fallback while keeping high-priority on Dedicated as long as capacity allows. we can also enforce soft timeouts — if the model take >200ms then route to a cheaper variant.
[07:28] Rajiv Menon: are those policy changes free or do they change cost? we need to understand pricing for partial fallbacks.
[07:35] Laura Chen: partial fallback doesn't incur additional fixed charges but it changes per-token cost because hosted rates differ. we'll provide an estimate for the actual mix from your traffic and show cost sensitivity.

[07:50] Carlos Ortiz: can we add an automatic model-variant fallback? e.g., when the quantized variant is causing issues route to a lower-memory variant with slightly worse quality.
[07:59] Marcus Patel: yes, variant fallback is a first-class feature. we can define compatibility sets so when the chosen variant hits memory constraints, requests will fall back to a compatible variant. that will be part of the rollout plan.

[08:15] Sophie Park: ok, on the action items — we'll start with TTL reduction and histogram exports, and you will push the heap-dump analysis.

[08:24] Marcus Patel: i will share the initial heap-dump analysis in a doc. quick preview: there are three hotspots — two in the attention kernel and one in the cudnn allocator path. initial patch idea: add a limiter for tracked allocations and enforce periodic release after N tokens for long-lived sessions.
[08:45] Rajiv Menon: sounds good. what about regression testing? we dont want quality regressions after changing cache TTL.
[08:52] Laura Chen: good point — Redwood Optimize can run your prompt set against the TTL-reduced environment to check for quality drift; we can run a 200-sample A/B and produce diff metrics.

[09:04] Nina Gomez: i'll coordinate and include the eval artifacts in the postmortem doc.

[09:12] Carlos Ortiz: small note on logs — during the incident our logs were noisy and some application logs were dropped due toebackpressure, any recs?
[09:21] Marcus Patel: we recommend a buffered logging pipeline with forwarder-side backpressure handling and also slotted log retention to S3. we had a transient sending error that caused the dropped lines. we'll add diagnostic flags to capture those lines in the next canary.

[09:36] Rajiv Menon: can we get an SLA addendum to cover fallback windows? something that guarantees a maximum fallback time or at least a notification timeline?
[09:44] Laura Chen: for Dedicated customers we have SLA targets; we can propose an addendum that includes faster failover windows for an incremental fee. i'll loop in sales/legal and provide a draft.

[10:00] Ava Li: one more risk question — if we increase eviction and GC frequency will that increase tail latencies? we need to balance memory and P99.
[10:09] Marcus Patel: there is a tradeoff. more aggressive GC can bump short-term P99 but prevent catastrophic OOM events; our approach is staged: first reduce TTL to lower baseline, then enable compaction in off-peak windows, and only increase GC frequency if metrics indicate it's safe. we will run microbenchmarks to quantify P50/P90/P99 tradeoffs.

[10:30] Sophie Park: are there any known interactions with our k8s node driver version? we are on 1.25 with a custom nvidia driver from Feb.
[10:39] Marcus Patel: we noted some kernel-level pinned pages in the kernel trace and there is a known issue with that driver version and cuda 12.2. patching drivers can be disruptive; we'll recommend a controlled node upgrade in the canary plan.

[10:55] Laura Chen: let's recap decisions and owners quickly so everyone is aligned.
[11:00] Action recap:
- ttl change to 30m for KV cache (Sophie to apply; Redwood to provide patch)
- Prometheus slope-based alert (Marcus to export rule)
- Heap-dump and kernel-trace analysis (Marcus to deliver summary)
- Canary plan for kernel fix + node driver upgrade (Marcus + Carlos to run; target 2025-11-26)
- Cost impact estimate and SLA addendum draft (Laura to send)
- Security audit snippets + KMS/HSM confirmation (Laura to share with Ava; due 2025-11-19)

[11:40] Rajiv Menon: that sums it up. thanks for the clear plan. one ask: can we get a short executive summary for our leadership that distills impact and mitigation in one page?
[11:52] Nina Gomez: yes, i'll draft a one-pager and include key metrics: cost delta, downtime avoided, mitigation ETA.

[12:04] Laura Chen: ok wrapping — next scheduled touch is 2025-11-26 for the canary validation but we'll share the heap analysis sooner. thanks everyone.

[12:12] Meeting end.

Notes and links:
- artifacts: https://redwood.s3/shared/polaris/heap-dump-11-14.bin (heap dump), https://redwood.s3/shared/polaris/kernel-trace-11-14.txt (kernel trace), https://redwood.app/patches/kv-ttl-diff-2025-11-17 (helm diff)
- postmortem doc link: https://redwood.docs/polaris/postmortem-memory-growth-2025-11-17 (draft)

Transcription quirks: occasional mis-labeling of K V cache as K V C, some proper nouns garbled (openlm as open lm), filler words preserved.
